candidates.headline: Least-loaded decoding dispatch does not imply or guarantee minimal TPOT when KV-cache transfer and memory are coupled
candidates.claim: DistServe's least-loaded decoding dispatch uses instance load as a proxy for decoding capacity; because KV-cache size, transfer delay, and memory pressure are coupled to decoding, the least-loaded instance may not be the one that minimizes TPOT.
candidates.paper_fact: All incoming requests arrive at a centralized controller, then dispatched to the prefill instance with the shortest queue for prefill processing, followed by dispatch to the least loaded decoding instance for decoding steps.
candidates.premise: Load metrics that ignore memory footprint and data-transfer dependencies can misrank instances; KV-cache size scales with context length and affects decoding memory and transfer time.
candidates.inference: Least-loaded decoding dispatch is not sufficient to guarantee TPOT SLOs when KV caches are large or transfers are bursty, because load may not reflect pending KV-cache memory or transfer backpressure.
candidates.toy_example: Toy example (not a measurement): two decoding instances report equal load, but one has many large KV caches pending transfer; choosing the least-loaded by request count may not minimize TPOT.
candidates.conditional_consequence: If contexts are long, KV caches are large, or cross-node bandwidth is limited, least-loaded dispatch can still overload decoding memory or incur transfer delay; if contexts are short and bandwidth high, the proxy is more reliable.
candidates.critical_link: The critical link is the assumption that the load metric captures the decoding instance's ability to accept and process KV caches without memory or transfer delay.
necessary_conditions: Variable KV-cache sizes across requests
Limited decoding memory or KV-transfer bandwidth
A load metric that does not fully account for pending KV-cache memory or transfer work
defeaters: Uniform short contexts with small KV caches
High-bandwidth placement that makes transfer negligible
A load metric that includes KV-cache memory and transfer backlog
do_not_infer: Do not infer that the paper claims least-loaded dispatch guarantees minimal TPOT.
Do not infer a measured TPOT regression from this reasoning alone.
Do not infer that least-loaded dispatch is always worse than other simple policies.
author_boundaries: Authors report least-loaded decoding dispatch and pull-based KV transfer.
Authors do not claim the load metric captures all KV-cache memory or transfer effects.

candidates.paper_fact: In DistServe, the FCFS policy can lead to a “convoy effect”, where longer requests block shorter ones in the prefill stage.
candidates.premise: Non-preemptive FCFS can cause head-of-line blocking; bursty arrivals increase queueing and memory pressure, and long requests can delay short ones.
candidates.inference: Simple FCFS dispatch does not by itself guarantee latency SLOs when arrivals are bursty and request lengths are mixed; the paper's own convoy-effect and burstiness discussion identifies conditions where the mechanism can degrade.
candidates.toy_example: Toy example (not a measurement): a burst of long prompts arrives just before many short prompts; FCFS prefill processing lets the long prompts block the short ones, increasing short-request TTFT.
candidates.conditional_consequence: If burstiness is high and long requests are frequent, tail latency and decoding-memory overload risk rise; if arrivals are smooth and requests are short or uniform, the risk is lower.
candidates.critical_link: The critical link is the non-preemptive FCFS ordering combined with bursty arrivals and variable service times.
necessary_conditions: Bursty or clustered request arrivals
Mixed request lengths with long requests present
No preemption or priority scheduling in the prefill path
defeaters: Smooth Poisson-like arrivals with low burstiness
Uniform short requests
Preemption or length-aware scheduling added on top of FCFS
Sufficient decoding memory and KV-transfer buffering
do_not_infer: Do not infer that DistServe fails all bursty workloads.
Do not infer a measured SLO violation beyond what the paper reports.
Do not infer that FCFS is the only cause of any SLO miss.
author_boundaries: Authors explicitly report the FCFS convoy effect and absence of preemption.
Authors do not claim FCFS guarantees SLO attainment under burstiness; they leave preemption as future work.

quotes.quote: In DistServe, the FCFS policy can lead to a “convoy effect”, where longer requests block shorter ones in the prefill stage.
DistServe does not implement advanced runtime policies like preemption [26] and fault tolerance [58], which are complementary to disaggregation.
Burstiness in workloads can cause a deluge of KV caches to transfer from prefill to decoding instances, risking memory overload on decoding instances.

candidates.mechanism: Non-preemptive FCFS can cause head-of-line blocking; bursty arrivals increase queueing and memory pressure, and long requests can delay short ones. candidates.headline: Disaggregation does not imply goodput improvement in throughput-optimized or resource-constrained deployments.
candidates.claim: Disaggregation's goodput benefit is conditional on latency-sensitive SLOs and enough GPUs; it does not imply improvement for offline throughput or single-GPU deployments.
candidates.paper_fact: In offline applications that are not latency-sensitive, users typically have lower requirements for response time [45]. This allows serving systems to shift focus towards maximizing overall throughput instead of goodput and the effectiveness of DistServe may be compromised.
candidates.premise: Goodput optimization targets latency SLO attainment; offline throughput may prefer full batches and colocation; separating phases requires multiple GPUs and extra weight copies.
candidates.inference: The mechanism's advantage is not universal; in those regimes colocated or chunked-prefill systems may be preferable.
candidates.conditional_consequence: If the workload is offline/throughput-oriented or only one/few GPUs are available, disaggregation may add complexity without goodput gain; condition on SLO sensitivity and GPU count.
candidates.critical_link: Benefit depends on removing interference that matters for latency SLOs and on having enough resources to allocate separate phase instances.
necessary_conditions: Latency-sensitive TTFT/TPOT SLOs
Multiple GPUs or instances
Mixed prefill/decode workload
Ability to replicate model weights per phase
defeaters: Offline throughput target
Single GPU or very few GPUs
Resource-constrained deployment
Simpler colocated system may be preferred
Paper reports goodput gains in evaluated latency-sensitive settings
do_not_infer: Do not infer disaggregation never improves throughput
Do not infer it is always worse in small clusters
Do not infer paper's gains apply to offline serving

quotes.quote: In offline applications that are not latency-sensitive, users typically have lower requirements for response time [45]. This allows serving systems to shift focus towards maximizing overall throughput instead of goodput and the effectiveness of DistServe may be compromised.
In resource-constrained scenarios, such as environments with only a few or even a single GPU, the design space for DistServe is significantly limited.
In this case, simpler architectural choices like non-disaggregated systems [3, 32] may reduce deployment complexity and optimize operational efficiency.
